name: Off-grid skills
desc: Making fire, cooking without power, keeping food safe, simple shelter, drinking water, toilet and light without power, staying warm

s: Check the rules: in summer many regions (also in Italy) ban open fires outside, with big fines.
Pick bare ground or a ring of stones, away from tents, dry grass and overhanging branches. Clear about 3 metres around it.
Keep water, sand or earth ready to put it out.
Keep the fire small and never leave it alone.
To put it out: pour water, stir the ashes, pour again, until everything is cold to the touch.
d: Never burn a fire or charcoal indoors without a chimney: it makes carbon monoxide, which you can't see or smell
Don't use petrol to light a fire

s: Collect three piles, all as dry as possible: tinder (dry grass, birch bark, paper, cotton wool), kindling (twigs as thin as a pencil) and fuel (sticks as thick as your wrist).
Collect twice as much as you think you need, before you start.
Put a fist-sized ball of tinder in the middle and lean kindling around it like a small tent (teepee).
Light the tinder low down, on the side the wind comes from.
Blow gently at the base when it catches.
Add bigger wood slowly, a few pieces at a time, leaving gaps for air.
d: Don't smother it with big wood too early

s: Ferro rod (fire steel): hold it into the tinder and scrape the striker down along it firmly to throw sparks.
Battery and steel wool: touch both poles of a 9V battery to fine steel wool; it glows. Put it straight into tinder.
Sun and a lens: a magnifying glass or reading glasses focus sunlight to a small bright dot on dark, dry tinder. Hold still.
Keep matches and a lighter in a waterproof bag in your kit, so you don't need any of this.
d: Keep steel wool away from batteries in your bag

s: Let the fire burn down for 20–30 minutes until you have glowing embers: they give even heat, flames burn food.
Put the pan on two flat stones or a grate over the embers.
Foil packets: wrap food (potatoes, vegetables, fish) in two layers of foil and lay it in the embers. Turn it now and then.
One-pot meals are easiest: pasta, rice, soup, stew.
Boil drinking water first while the fire is hottest.
d: Don't use stones from a river or sea right next to the fire: wet stones can crack

guides.t: Cooking when the power is out
guides.w: Gas, barbecue or no cooking at all
s: A camping gas stove or barbecue works without power, but only use it outside or on an open balcony.
No-cook meals: bread, tins (fish, beans), cheese, nuts, fruit. Keep a tin opener that works by hand.
Save fuel with a ‘hay box’: boil the pot for a few minutes, then wrap it in blankets or a sleeping bag. It keeps cooking slowly (rice, pasta, stews).
Gas hobs often still work: light them with a match.
d: Never use a barbecue, camping stove or generator indoors
guides.src: Fire service & carbon monoxide safety advice

guides.w: Fridge and freezer in a power cut
s: Keep the fridge and freezer doors closed as much as you can. Decide what you need, then open it once.
A closed fridge stays cold for about 4 hours. A full freezer keeps food frozen for about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.
Help it: put bottles of water or ice packs in the freezer now, and fill gaps with them. In winter, a cool box outside in the shade works as a fridge (below 7 °C).
Eat the food from the fridge first, then the freezer, then tins and dry food.
A fridge thermometer tells you the truth: above 7 °C for more than 4 hours means throw away meat, fish, eggs, milk, soft cheese and leftovers.
When the power comes back: frozen food with ice crystals left or still at 4 °C or colder can be refrozen. Fully thawed meat or fish: cook it and eat it, or throw it out.
d: Don't taste food to check if it's still safe
When in doubt, throw it out

guides.w: Out of wind and rain, off the cold ground
s: Pick a spot that's flat and dry, out of the wind. Not in a dry riverbed and not under dead branches.
Lean-to: tie or wedge a strong pole between two trees at chest height.
Lean branches against one side of the pole, closely together, with the back to the wind.
Cover it thickly with leaves, ferns or a tarp. Thicker is drier.
With a tarp: hang a rope between two trees, put the tarp over it like a tent and peg or weigh down the corners.
Make a thick bed of leaves or branches to lie on: the cold ground takes more heat than the air. Keep it small: small is warmer.
Best: bottled water, or tap water if the water company says it's safe.
Boiling is the surest way: bring it to a rolling boil and keep it boiling for 1 minute (3 minutes high in the mountains). Let it cool covered.
Cloudy water: let it stand so the dirt sinks, pour off the top, and filter it through a clean cloth or coffee filter before treating it.

Household bleach (plain, unscented, about 5 %): 2 drops per litre of clear water, stir, wait 30 minutes. It should smell slightly of chlorine; if not, repeat and wait again. Double it for cloudy or cold water.
Purification tablets work too: follow the waiting time on the pack (often 30 minutes, longer when the water is cold).
No fuel and lots of sun: fill clear plastic bottles (max. 2 litres) with clear water and leave them lying in full sun for 6 hours (2 days when cloudy).
Keep treated water in clean, closed bottles or jerrycans, and use a clean cup to scoop it.
d: Don't drink sea water or water from near fields that have been sprayed
Filters alone don't make water safe unless they say they remove bacteria and viruses: boil it too

s: Cut the bottom off a plastic bottle and put it upside down, cap with a small hole at the bottom.
Fill it in layers from the bottom up: cloth, crushed charcoal from a fire, fine sand, coarse sand, small stones.
Pour the water in slowly and collect it below. Pour it through again if it's still cloudy.
Then BOIL it: a filter like this removes dirt, not the germs that make you sick.
d: Don't drink filtered water without boiling it

guides.w: Store it before you need it
s: Keep 3 litres per person per day, for at least 3 days.
When a cut is announced, fill bottles, pots and the bath (bath water for washing and the toilet).
The hot-water tank of a boiler holds clean water too.
Collect rainwater in clean buckets; boil it before drinking.
Flush the toilet with a bucket of used water.
Live in one small room, preferably on the sunny side, and keep its doors closed. Close curtains as soon as it gets dark.
Stop draughts: a rolled-up towel along the door, blankets or bubble wrap over windows.
Wear layers (thin ones trap more warmth than one thick one), a hat, gloves and thick socks, also in bed.
Put blankets or rugs on the floor and under you in bed: you lose more heat downwards than upwards.
Hot-water bottles, warm drinks and hot food help a lot. Move about every hour, and sleep close together.
Check on babies, older people and anyone ill: they get cold without noticing. Shivering that stops, confusion or sleepiness can be hypothermia.
Candles and oil lamps: on a plate, away from curtains, never left alone. A torch is safer.
d: Never heat a room with a barbecue, camping stove, gas oven or generator: carbon monoxide can kill you in your sleep
guides.src: Fire service & carbon monoxide safety advice

guides.t: Toilet and washing without running water
guides.w: When the toilet won't flush for days
s: A few days: flush the toilet with a bucket of used water (bath or washing-up water), poured in quickly.
No water at all: make a bucket toilet. Put two strong bin bags in a bucket or in the toilet bowl itself.
After each use, cover it with a scoop of sawdust, cat litter or dry soil. It stops the smell and the flies. Keep a lid on.
Pee separately in a bottle or another bucket if you can: the bags stay much drier and lighter.
Tie the bag when it's a third full and store it outside in a closed bin, away from water and food, until it can be collected.
Wash your hands after the toilet and before eating: a little water and soap, or hand gel. A bottle with a small hole makes a tap.
Dishes: scrape them clean, wash in one bowl and rinse in a second with boiled water. Keep drinking water separate from washing water.
d: Don't let toilet waste near a well, a ditch or your water store
Don't skip hand washing: stomach bugs spread fast when water is short

guides.t: Lighting your home in a blackout
s: Best: torches and head torches with spare batteries. A head torch leaves your hands free.
Solar garden lights: put them in the sun by day and bring them inside at night.
Make a torch light the whole room: point it at the ceiling, or put it under a jug or bottle of water.
Candles: in a stable holder on a plate, away from curtains, children and pets, and blow them out when you leave the room.
Camping gas lamps and oil lamps give off fumes: only outside or with a window open, never while sleeping.
Save light: one lamp in the room where everyone is, and go to bed earlier.
d: Never leave candles or lamps burning unattended
No gas lamp or heater in a bedroom
